answer.label: Not George Eliot — a persistent misattribution
answer.sourceLine: No evidence this exact sentence appears anywhere in George Eliot’s novels, essays, or letters. Researchers trace it instead to a reader’s unsourced submission to an 1881 magazine contest, likely echoing a line by poet Adelaide Anne Procter.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — widely repeated, but not found in George Eliot’s actual writing

source.excerpt: No star is ever lost we once have seen, / We always may be what we might have been.
trail: First printed with George Eliot’s name attached in an unsourced 1881 reader contest, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Full-text searches of Eliot’s novels (including Middlemarch, via the Project Gutenberg edition ↗) turn up no match for the line.
Eliot scholars consulted by fact-checkers, including a retired professor of English, confirmed the line is not authentic; see Check Your Fact’s report ↗.
The likely poetic root, Adelaide Anne Procter’s 1859 line “we always may be what we might have been,” can be read in context at this edition of the poem ↗.
source.excerptNote: The Procter couplet Quote Investigator identifies as the likely source of the later Eliot misattribution.
source.rightsNote: Because this exact sentence cannot be tied to any specific published work by an identifiable author, no public-domain or copyright status can be honestly assigned to it as a discrete text.

author.name: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans)
author.heading: About George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans)
author.bio: Mary Ann Evans wrote under the pen name George Eliot to be taken seriously in a literary world that dismissed women’s fiction as frivolous. Her novels, especially Middlemarch (1871–72), are ranked among the greatest in English literature for their psychological depth and moral seriousness — which is precisely why inspirational-sounding lines are so often pinned on her, whether she wrote them or not.

context.heading: How a magazine contest built a fake Eliot quote
lead: In June 1881, less than a year after George Eliot’s death, the magazine Literary News ran a reader contest to collect the “best” quotations from her work. One submission — entry 23, printed without any source citation — read “It is never too late to be what you might have been.” The editors did not verify it against Eliot’s actual books, and it has never been located in any of them since.

Quote Investigator, which traced the line’s history, suggests it may be a compressed rewording of a couplet by the poet Adelaide Anne Procter, published two decades earlier: “No star is ever lost we once have seen, / We always may be what we might have been.” Once printed under Eliot’s name in 1881, the line was copied forward by anthologies and, eventually, motivational posters and social media, with the wording gradually smoothing into today’s familiar form.
context.pull: Entry 23 in an 1881 fan contest, printed with no source — and it stuck for well over a century.
